issues.legal_issue: An appellate court should not disturb a supported factual finding about who contributed the purchase consideration absent perversity or a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The High Court reappraised the oral and documentary evidence and found that several family members contributed to the purchase consideration, while the person named in the sale deed had not proved that he paid it all.
The evidence included bank records and testimony that the demand draft was purchased from an account funded in substantial part by another family member.
The Supreme Court found no perversity or miscarriage of justice in the High Court’s assessment.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court’s factual finding that the consideration was contributed by the family members and not provided by the named purchaser alone.
issues.legal_principle: A factual finding by the last court of fact is not to be reappraised or reversed in an appeal absent perversity or an approach causing miscarriage of justice; the finding here was a pure finding of fact.

rule.if: civil_appeal_from_fact_finding and evidence_supports_shared_contributions and not finding_perverse and not miscarriage_of_justice

predicates.civil_appeal_from_fact_finding: The proceeding is an appeal that challenges a factual finding made by a lower court.
predicates.evidence_supports_shared_contributions: The evidence supports that persons besides the named purchaser contributed to the purchase consideration.
predicates.finding_perverse: The challenged factual finding is perverse in light of the evidence.
predicates.miscarriage_of_justice: The challenged finding or the approach used to reach it caused a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a factual finding, evidence supports the finding, and neither perversity nor miscarriage of justice is present, the appellate court upholds the finding.

issues.legal_issue: The prohibition on asserting rights in property held in another person’s name does not bar a claim where the named holder held the property in a fiduciary capacity for the claimants’ benefit.
material_facts: The property had been occupied by a deceased family member as a tenant, and the family members’ tenancy interests would ordinarily have devolved on her legal heirs.
The property was transferred into one heir’s name because the public authority required transfer to a single individual, not because the other heirs had abandoned their interests.
The other family members continued to evince an interest in the property and contributed, along with their father, to the purchase consideration.
The family members were closely related, and the claimants continued in possession of the property.
The suit to establish co-ownership was filed after the legislation took effect, although the sale deed had been executed earlier.
issues.conclusion: The transaction fell within the fiduciary-capacity exception, so the suit was not barred by the prohibition on recovering property held benami.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 4(1), (2) and (3)(b) of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 apply to a post-enactment suit concerning property transferred before enactment, subject to the statutory exception for property held by a trustee or another person in a fiduciary capacity for another’s benefit. A fiduciary relationship connotes trust and confidence on one side and good faith on the other, and may extend beyond technical trustee relationships; its existence is determined from the factual context. The Court relied on Central Board of Secondary Education v. Adiya Bandopadhyay (2011) 8 SCC 497 for the meaning of fiduciary relationship. The High Court had also referred to Section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, but the Supreme Court affirmed the result on the fiduciary exception.

predicates.ownership_claim_against_named_holder: A claimant brings a suit asserting an ownership right in property held in another person’s name.
predicates.property_held_for_claimants_benefit: The property was held for the benefit of the claimant or claimants.
predicates.named_holder_in_fiduciary_capacity: The person named as holder occupied a position of trust and confidence toward the claimant or claimants in relation to the property.

issues.definition: An ownership claim against a named holder is not barred when that holder held the property for the claimants’ benefit in a fiduciary capacity.

issues.legal_issue: A party may rely on a fiduciary-capacity exception on appeal when the statutory bar was already in issue, the exception requires no new factual findings, and considering it causes no failure of justice.
material_facts: The appellant relied on the statutory prohibition before the High Court, and the respondents relied on the fiduciary exception to defend the maintainability of their suit.
The fiduciary issue could be decided using facts already found by the High Court, without additional factual findings.
The Supreme Court found that considering the exception did not surprise the appellant and that there was no failure of justice.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were entitled to rely on the fiduciary-capacity exception even though they had not raised it before the lower courts.
issues.legal_principle: A defensive legal answer to an issue raised by the opposing party is not impermissibly new where the issue was already argued, no additional facts are needed, and considering the answer causes no failure of justice.

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and opposing_party_invoked_statutory_bar and defense_relies_on_existing_findings and not additional_facts_required and not failure_of_justice

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is before a court hearing an appeal.
predicates.opposing_party_invoked_statutory_bar: The opposing party raised a statutory bar to the claim before the appellate court or a lower court.
predicates.defense_relies_on_existing_findings: The defense to the bar relies on facts already found in the proceedings.
predicates.additional_facts_required: Additional factual findings are needed to decide the defense to the bar.
predicates.failure_of_justice: Considering the defense at the appellate stage would cause a failure of justice.

issues.definition: In an appeal, the court may consider a defense to a statutory bar when the bar was invoked, the defense relies on existing findings, and neither additional facts nor a failure of justice is involved.
